props.title: Together Alone

sections.content: **Together Alone** (1991) stands as a pivotal entry in New Queer Cinema, arriving at the height of the AIDS crisis. Director P.J. Castellaneta crafted this intimate chamber piece with just two actors and one location, predating similar minimalist dialogue-driven films like **Before Sunrise** (1995). Shot in stark black and white for $7,000, the film follows one night's conversation between two men after a sexual encounter, touching themes that would later emerge in **Weekend** (2011) and **Looking** (2014).

sections.content: The film's technical constraints - single location, real-time dialogue, minimalist staging - create an intimacy that influenced later LGBTQ+ cinema. **My Beautiful Laundrette** (1985) and **Maurice** (1987) had already proven gay narratives could reach mainstream audiences, but **Together Alone** stripped away period settings and production values to focus purely on human connection.

Castellaneta's approach to filming intimate conversation would echo through independent cinema, seen in works like **Medicine for Melancholy** (2008) and **In Search of a Midnight Kiss** (2007). The film's exploration of casual encounters evolving into deeper connection presaged similar themes in **Shortbus** (2006) and **Keep the Lights On** (2012). sections.content: The legacy of **Together Alone** (1991) is evident in contemporary films that embrace similar constraints. **Blue Jay** (2016) uses black and white photography and extended dialogue to explore connection, while **Malcolm & Marie** (2021) confines its relationship drama to a single location. These films prove the enduring power of Castellaneta's minimalist approach.
